divisions.question: Debate resumed. Helen Kroger I will resume from where I left off earlier on in the day in making some observations about the [Education Legislation Amendment Bill 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3057) and the [Schools Assistance Bill 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3093). I was referring to an article published in the _Canberra Times_ on 6 November 2008. The author was Rabbi Kennard, who is the Principal of Mount Scopus Memorial College in Melbourne—a very well known school. He made some very pertinent observations. He said: Does the “compulsory” nature of the curriculum mean that Australia will follow the (no doubt caricatured) French model, whereby the minister of education could look at his watch and know what each child throughout his country would be studying? Will it follow the English system, where teachers were told exactly how to spend each minute of the daily “Literacy Hour” and could expect school inspectors to check-up that the first 20 minutes was spent in direct teaching, followed by the correct amount of group work and summation? Or will the curriculum be closer to the Victorian system, which schools highly support? The Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority has devised the Victorian Essential Learning Standards, a “curriculum framework” which in detail describes the areas that students must be taught and the standards that they are expected to reach, while still allowing principals and teachers the right to exercise their professional judgment as to how best to achieve these results. Rabbi Kennard, may I proffer, is only one of many principals of independent schools that are mightily concerned about the Schools Assistance Bill 2008. Despite Minister Gillard’s claims of an education revolution in the last 12 months, I have to confess that I am an education revolution sceptic. What she has demonstrated in the la

[EDUCATION LEGISLATION AMENDMENT BILL 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3057) Bill—by leave—taken as a whole. Claire Moore The question is that the bill stand as printed. Question agreed to. [SCHOOLS ASSISTANCE BILL 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3093) Bill—by leave—taken as a whole. Ian Macdonald Before we move to the bill, I see the advisers are not yet here. Kim Carr We will help you. Ian Macdonald Minister, you have already indicated that you will give me the assurances which I sought. I thought that if I could get those assurances and just understand on what basis those assurances are given then I will be out of the debate and will leave it to people who have a lot of amendments and other issues to raise. But, Minister, I would not accept you are well versed and competent to do it, and I will say a few things while your officials are getting here. I am very concerned, on advice from those involved, that this bill will mean a massive reduction in funding for Catholic boarding schools, particularly in the diocese of Townsville, which are the schools that educate the greatest number of Indigenous people in Australia. Whilst I do not assume bad faith on the part of the government, and I mentioned that in the debate—my contribution is not political, although the minister was clearly incapable of understanding that and could not help himself but pretend that we were back in the old bullyboy union days where you had to attack anyone who had a view that might be slightly different to yours; my contribution had nothing to do with that—my contribution is to try to assist the government to do what I do not think they meant to do, and that is to ensure that these Indigenous schools do not suffer with respect to funding. speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The speaker moved that the bills be taken together and read a first time without formalities, and the motion was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The speech announced the introduction of several bills, including education legislation that appropriates over $0.5 billion for Indigenous education programs from 2009 to 2012, and a Schools Assistance Bill providing $28 billion for non-government schools, with a focus on closing Indigenous educational gaps. It also introduced revised heavy vehicle registration charges to end cross-subsidisation, a road user charge increase to 21 cents per litre, and a $70 million Heavy Vehicle Safety and Productivity Package.

speeches.speaker: Brett Mason
speeches.brief: The Schools Assistance Bill 2008 provides $28 billion for non-government schools (2009–2012) but the opposition raised four objections: new ministerial power to withhold funding based on a qualified audit; mandatory compliance with an unfinished national curriculum; expanded reporting of all school funding sources, risking misuse; and abolition of establishment grants for new non-government schools. The Education Legislation Amendment Bill 2008, which consolidates Indigenous education programs into one per capita payment worth $742.6 million, was supported by the opposition despite concerns about potential disadvantage for remote Indigenous boarding students.

speeches.speaker: Helen Kroger
speeches.brief: Senator Macdonald argued that the Education Legislation Amendment Bill 2008 and Schools Assistance Bill 2008 would financially disadvantage Indigenous boarding schools in North Queensland, specifically naming St Patrick's College, Abergowrie College, Columba Catholic College, and Shalom College, by shifting funding from "remote students" to "remote schools." He also criticised the government's education record, citing $400 million in program cuts and an $800 million cost blowout for the computer program.

speeches.speaker: Claire Moore
speeches.brief: Senator Ian Macdonald argued that the Schools Assistance Bill 2008 would cause a substantial reduction in funding for Catholic boarding schools in Queensland, particularly those educating Indigenous students, and sought an assurance that schools like Abergowrie College, Columba College, St Patrick’s College, and others would not receive less funding over the next four years, indexed for inflation.

speeches.speaker: Kim Carr
speeches.brief: The government argued that the Schools Assistance Bill 2008 is essential for accountability and transparency in schools, linking it to a national curriculum and $28 billion in funding over four years. Opposition amendments removed funding ties to the embryonic national curriculum, added provisions for Indigenous students from remote areas, and protected donor privacy.
